The consensus had clearly 27 broken down and the constitutional structures that were designed 28 to foster consensus had also broken down. 2 MR. ORIE: Professor Hayden, is this reference to the constitutional structure a reference to the prohibition to outvote other peoples? Is this a reference to the right of secession for the peoples, each of it, each of the constituent parties, in that Republic? Is that what you say, that what Badinter proposed finally turned out to be unconstitutional -- at least suggested, I should not, when I listen well to you, he did not propose a referendum but he suggested that possibly that might be of some help and it finally turned out to be unconstitutional as it was held. 12 A. I would have to ponder the constitutionality of it in regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Certainly, the way it was scheduled in regard to Badinter's suggestion seems to have been brought about unconstitutionally. To schedule this referendum that Badinter had suggested was not done in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the parliamentary manoeuvring sounds extremely dubious as well. 19 Q. Professor Hayden, I will come back to the consistency of Badinter in his opinions 4, 8 and 11 that have been presented to you. Could you explain whether there are any inconsistencies in these subsequent opinions? 23 A. Opinion No. 4 -- I am sorry, opinion No. 8 ---- 24 Q. If you refer to specific parts, I would like you to put it on the ---- 26 A. Yes, I would have to find them to do this. It is dated July 4th of 1992. Right, clause 3 -- I do not have it on my monitor. I 28 do not know if you have it on yours. There we are. Yes, OK. The referendum proposed in opinion No. 4 was held -- proposed, yes, OK -- on 29th February/1 March a large majority of the population voted in favour of the Republics independence. This is a statement of July 4th. That is opinion No. 8. As for No. 11 -- I am sorry, I have to find this. 7 Q. I think 11 was 54. 8 A. Yes. It is paragraph 6. OK. "In opinion No. 4 issued on 11 January, the Arbitration Commission came to the view that 'the will of the peoples ... could not be held to have been fully established'. Since then, in a referendum held ... the majority of the people have expressed themselves in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia". I find that a significant difference in wording, "the majority of the people", as opposed to "the will of the peoples". 16 Q. Professor Hayden, could this difference in wording perhaps be explained by the situation that existed at the time the opinion No. 11 was delivered compared, for example, to the time when opinion 4 was delivered? 20 A. I would suggest that that is probably so. Opinion 4 was written in January of 1992 and the question was whether recognition should be granted. Opinion 8 was written in January -- in July. 11, also after that. Recognition had been granted in April, so that recognition was a fait accompli. Badinter was then confronted with a situation in which, if he were to maintain his original criterion, the political decision to recognise would have been mistaken, and I do not wish to impute 28 anything to Mr. Badinter but I do find the circumstances to be significant. 3 Q. Professor Hayden, in your opinion and applying the Badinter definition of a state as a community which consists of a territory and a population subject to an organised political authority, was by late 1991 Bosnia and Herzegovina empirically a state or not? 8 A. By those criteria, certainly by early 1992 on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were three communities, not one, there was no single community. Organised political authority, as defined by the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had clearly broken down. Thus I would say that by the Badinter criteria Bosnia was not empirically a state after that time. 14 Q. Professor Hayden, your testimony seems to indicate that the processes that took place throughout the former Yugoslavia and brought about this dissolution, also took place within Bosnia-Herzegovina and led similarly to the dissolution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you perhaps point out the main points whether this really is what your statement is? 20 A. Yes, I think that is the essence of my statement and I might simply provide a summation. Yugoslavia was created was created after World War I and the basic premise of Yugoslavia was that the South Slavic peoples were so closely related to each other that they could co-existed, so intermingled that they had to co-exist. Empirically both of these were true. However, that is not what won in the free and fair elections of 1990. What succeeded state socialism in Yugoslavia in 1990 was the separate 28 1 nationalisms of the Yugoslav peoples, the narodi, nationalisms 2 by which each people would get its own state; the narod, the 3 ethnic group in American terms, gets the state, the territory 4 and the government. This is what won in 1990, this is what 5 people voted for. Voting for this, this construction is 6 possible if not exactly admirable as I think Judge McDonald 7 suggested yesterday in a question to me. In most of the Yugoslav Republics the problem is in 9 Bosnia and Herzegovina where there was no majority narod in whom 10 sovereignty could reside. Bosnia and Herzegovina could have 11 existed as a state under this political definition if the 12 population of Bosnia and Herzegovina chose to view themselves as 13 Bosnians. I think quite tragically in the free and fair 14 elections in 1990 they did not. They partitioned themselves 15 into Serbs, Croats, Muslims and others which, of course, the 16 possibility was always there, the presence of these groups was 17 always there. Groups with strikingly, peoples in Yugoslav terms, 19 narods, with strikingly different views of what the future of 20 Bosnia and Herzegovina should be, with some of them certainly 21 the dominant Serbian political opinion, and quickly the dominant 22 Croatian political opinion in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was that, 23 as the Yugoslav Constitutions had said, it was the narod that 24 had the right to self-determination and that they had the right, 25 as Slovenia and Croatian had seceded from Yugoslavia, to secede 26 from Bosnia and Herzegovina and did not want to be included in 27 this state. The constitutional and political structures devised 28 1 to prevent this type of breakdown in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did 2 not function and the constitutional order of the state 3 dissolved, leaving these three communities. I find this a situation in which civil war was 5 absolutely inevitable for one of two reasons. If Bosnia were to 6 be constituted as a state empirically within its borders in the 7 former Yugoslavia, it would have been opposed militarily on 8 those peoples who rejected it, or alternatively they had made 9 it, both the Serbs and the Croats, quite clear that they would 10 fight to avoid being included in the state that they rejected, 11 and that is indeed what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour. I have a just 13 technical issue, but first if you want to put any additional 14 questions?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, it was just one question really. 16 I suppose it relates to history and you have said you are not a 17 historian. You have taken us from World War I, at the close of 18 World War I, when this state of Yugoslavia was created and then 19 you take us to free elections. Well, you talked a little bit 20 before that, 1989 the amendments to the Constitution in 21 Slovenia, then Croatia and then of course in 1990, in 1991 we 22 get to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you tell us what was the 23 role of Tito or the effect that Tito's reign, so to speak, 24 during that interim period after World War II, and how perhaps 25 Tito either as an individual or the way that the Constitutions 26 were structured was able to hold these divergent narods 27 together? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the basic principles of Tito's Yugoslavia, as I think 2 I said when I read those extracts from the Slovenian 3 intellectuals, one of the basic principles was brotherhood and 4 unity, bratstvo-jedinstvo, that Slovenian intellectuals at the 5 time, by the late 80s, were rejecting, brotherhood as terror and 6 unity as homogenization and they rejected this. Tito and the 7 partisans were very aware of what the consequences of a 8 breakdown of Yugoslavia would be. World War II in Yugoslavia 9 had been, among other things, a quite ghastly civil war which in 10 terms of numbers of victims, absolute numbers of victims on a 11 smaller population base, was much worse than what we have seen 12 in Yugoslavia since 1991. Tito and the partisans having thought that, and this 14 was part of it, it was a war against occupiers but there were 15 some ghastly civil wars and what they interpreted as a communist 16 revolution all going on simultaneously. I would say that we 17 have not seen anything in Bosnia since 1991 that we did not see 18 in Bosnia between 1941 and 1945. Tito and company were aware of 19 this and this is why they set up a federal state. Their idea 20 was to give maximum autonomy to these nations so that none would 21 feel constrained. What happened was that from the first 22 Constitution of 1945 until the last Constitution in 1974, and 23 there was also effectively a new Constitution in '54, there was 24 one in '63, the constitutional structures became so loose that 25 it became a de facto confederation which then Slovenia and 26 Croatia used to bring down the entire structure. I might address it in another way. The problems of 28 1 Bosnia and Herzegovina were certainly not new to the 1990s. As 2 I said, you a had civil war in the 1940s. People in Bosnia, if 3 I can use Bosnians, Bosanci as opposed to Bosnjaci, had lived 4 together for many centuries, but the centuries have been 5 punctuated by periods of violence and these have tended to occur 6 after the larger state that has encompassed Bosnia-Herzegovina 7 has collapsed or a state authority has been withdrawn. There 8 were periods when Bosnia was part of the Ottoman empire until 9 1878. When the Ottoman empire withdrew there was a great deal 10 of violence and many Muslims left for Turkey with the Otomans. 11 When Austro-Hungarian empire collapsed at then end of World 12 War I there was a great deal of ethnic violence. When the first 13 Yugoslavia collapsed in 1941 there was a great deal of ethnic 14 violence, and when the second Yugoslavia collapsed in 1991/1992 15 the division of the population was something that had certainly 16 occurred before and the results were something that had 17 certainly occurred before. There is a curious sense in which it 18 was the fear of all this that, in effect, forced the population 19 of Bosnia and Herzegovina to partition themselves looking for 20 safety in the numbers of their fellow narod and, thus, bringing 21 about the destruction of the common state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that really it was the force or was it the force of Tito's 23 personality that was able to hold the republics together, even 24 though by their Constitutions they were given significant or a 25 modicum, I do not know whether it is significant, but some 26 independence and freedom, but the force of his personality 27 permitted the republics to stay together, is that so or not 28 1 so ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a sense ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: --- or is that an overstatement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. What permitted the republics to stay together was 5 the overarching structure of the communist party of Yugoslavia, 6 because you might have viewed the separate republics as being 7 almost administrative in character because political decisions 8 were made by the communist party of Yugoslavia. Tito could hold 9 this together. A part of the story of the disintegration of 10 communist Yugoslavia was also the disintegration of the League 11 of Communists of Yugoslavia into the Leagues of Communists of 12 each of the separate republics. This does not sound 13 unfamiliar. In the United States there is democratic party in 14 California and there is a Democratic party in New York and then 15 there is a democratic party of the United States of America, but 16 this structure was then seized by the Republican leaderships to 17 destroy the overarching federal party. At the same time that 18 the Slovenes were proclaiming the supremacy of the Republican 19 Constitution to the Federal Constitution, they were also 20 proclaiming the supremacy of the Republican party organisations 21 to those of the federal party. Tito certainly did not permit this to happen. 23 Something similar was on the verge of happening in 1971 and 24 Tito, largely through his personal authority, crushed it. The 25 structures that Tito left behind to deal with the potential 26 divisions of Yugoslavia, certainly were not adequate to the 27 task. 28 I can also say that throughout the 80s, which was where I started my testimony, there were people in Yugoslavia, very thoughtful people, who were aware of the inadequacies of the Tito structures, beginning with economics of course but then going through the political structures, and wished to revise them but they were defeated by the separate national elites in the separate republics. 8 Q. You said in 1910 that there were elections that really were divided according to ethnic lines. Is that not so? So, as early as then people were voting according to narods, their narods? 12 A. When the choice was given to vote more or less freely, then that is what they chose. 14 Q. Under Tito, under communism, that was kind of just swept under a rug or at least contained? 16 A. Well, elections were hardly free or fair in Tito's Yugoslavia. When I first went there in the early 80s one of the jokes people told me was that, "We don't have elections, we do have voting." 19 Q. So when that then disappeared and the former Yugoslavia had its first try at democracy in how many years would that have been? 21 A. Well, actually the last elections had been in the 1920s because of a dictatorship declared in 1929, so it was a long time. It was virtually 60 years. 24 Q. So when they had their first chance at democracy they reverted back to their ethnic differences, and superimposed really their parties on these ethnic groups or on their ethnic groups, I suppose, is that not so? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The parties that won were the ones were the parties were ethnic 2 parties. This is what won. Not all parties were ethnic 3 parties. As I said, in Bosnia particularly there was a party 4 headed by the Federal Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, a Croat 5 from Bosnia, who was trying desperately to hold Yugoslavia 6 together because he knew, as I can assure you everyone knew, 7 what the consequences would be. This was a non-ethnic party. 8 It was the League of the Reformists of Yugoslavia. It stood for 9 a civil society, a state of equal citizens. As I said, it got 10 about 6 per cent of the vote. That probably happened because 11 that election was in November and in the elections in Croatia in 12 May the Croatian Democratic Union had already won, had already 13 made perfectly clear its intention of seceding from Yugoslavia. 14 The Croatian Democratic Union that was active in Bosnia and 15 Herzegovina was and is controlled by the Croatian Democratic 16 Union in Zagreb. So that it already seemed as if the electorate 17 in Bosnia would fracture, that the chances of saving Yugoslavia 18 were non-existent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the conflict then was caused by what would you say, the 20 clashing claims for nationalism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the formulation accepted -- and that is not just Yugoslavia 22 but more or less throughout central Europe -- that the state, 23 the territory and the government, belongs to the one nation. As 24 I say, the problem with Bosnia was that it did not have one 25 nation in the Yugoslav sense. It had three. Remember that it 26 was the nations of Yugoslavia that had united. It was the 27 nations of Yugoslavia that had the right to self-determination 28 1 according to the Constitution and to the way that Yugoslavs 2 thought about these things and the way that their political 3 parties were operating. This meant that if the population of 4 Bosnia and Herzegovina turned itself into peoples instead of a 5 people, that it would be very difficult to envision how Bosnia 6 and Herzegovina could remain, because overwhelmingly the 7 political desire of the Croats of Herzegovina, if not the Croats 8 of Bosnia and there was a division there, was to become part of 9 Croatia. They were adjacent to Croatia. They felt themselves 10 to be part of Croatia. This has in fact happened. De facto 11 western Herzegovina is incorporated into the economic, 12 political, communications systems of Croatia. It is de facto 13 Croatia. This was clear that this was going to happen and it 14 was also clear that the Serbs were losing interest in Bosnia and 15 Herzegovina as well. In this type of structure being a member of a 17 minority, it is not simply a political minority. Our concepts 18 of democracy are based on the principle that the majority and 19 the minority can change. This is not the principle on which 20 these states are based. The principle on which these states are 21 based is that there is a permanent minority, and part of the 22 function of the state is to ensure the superiority, the 23 sovereignty of the majority. So that to be a member of a 24 minority in one of these states is to be outside of the body 25 sovereign, really in a sense outside of the body politic. This 26 was what won and everyone knew this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Each narod had a majority in one of the republics except the 28 Muslims? 2 A. That is correct, yes. 3 Q. So each Republic was free to express the sovereignty of its people, of its narods? 5 A. Yes, that is correct. 6 Q. Of the narods with giving superiority to the majority narod in Croatia, in Slovenia, in Serbia, but not in Bosnia-Herzegovina because they had 36 per cent I guess -- was it 36 per cent? 9 A. The Muslims by 1991 were approximately 44 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You are absolutely correct. 11 Q. So everyone was kind of going their separate way, and there were the narod, the Muslim narod in between with really no Republic to claim? 14 A. The only Republic they could claim would be Bosnia and Herzegovina in which they do not form a majority. For this reason there is very good evidence that the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the late 1980s was strongly in favour of the continuation of Yugoslavia, because they could see what would happen if Yugoslavia would disintegrate. There is good public survey data on this. In fact, the law on political organisations of Bosnia and Herzegovina prohibited the formation of political parties on an ethnic or national religious basis, in other words, a political party for a particular narod. There was very strong political support for this law in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1990, but it was clear after the Croatian elections in Croatia in 1990 the success of HDZ in Croatia and the success of the HDZ among Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina 28 1 that, you know, this picture was not going to work, that the 2 Croats were out, and the Serbs were as well, the Serbs and the 3 Croats actually had a very similar picture of Bosnia and 4 Herzegovina at this stage and they did not consider themselves 5 to be part of it. The Muslims actually took the same position 6 in regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Serbs took in 7 regard to Yugoslavia. The Serbs, as a Slovenian politician said 8 yesterday, in the excerpt that I read yesterday, he said the 9 downfall of Yugoslavia would be a catastrophe for the Serbs and 10 they knew it, and the downfall of Bosnia would be a catastrophe 11 for the Muslims and they knew that. But it would also be a 12 catastrophe for everyone in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are still trying to sort things out I suppose. With the 14 secession of Croatia, with the secession of Slovenia, what 15 Bosnia Herzegovina was left with was to stay in the federation 16 with Serbia. The Muslim narod was already a minority and if 17 they stayed in with the Serbian and Montenegrin they would be a 18 significant minority, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, and yet if they were to secede, then the other 20 groups could each feel themselves to be threatened as being in 21 the position of a minority. This was divined. You are quite 22 correct in starting it with the secession of Slovenia because 23 within the former Yugoslavia there was no majority narod. The 24 Serbs, like the Muslims in Bosnia, were about 45 per cent, maybe 25 even lower, overall because you had all of these other people. 26 The next largest group were the Croats, you have Muslims, 27 Slovenes, Muslims, Montenegrins, Macedonians. The others, and 28 1 Albanians actually, not one of the narodi, the narods of 2 Yugoslavia but 2 million Albanians in Serbia itself, so that 3 there was no majority. There was a whole set of institutional 4 structures that, well, we designed to promote consensus. As 5 I said, they were supposed to provide maximum autonomy and to 6 operate on consensus and they broke down, as similar mechanisms 7 broke down in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so the ones in Bosnia and 8 Herzegovina were patterned after federal ones. Slovenia's secession, you see, upset the demographic 10 balance because there are suddenly 2 million less non-Serbs 11 which would then increase, it increases the percentage of every 12 population left, but it would increase the percentage of Serbs 13 to the point where they would start to be close to being a 14 majority nation which the others might then fear. Of course it 15 certainly upset all of the political and constitutional 16 structures of Federal Yugoslavia, just as those Bosnia later 17 required participation and consensus, for this reason that in 18 1989 when I saw the Slovenian amendments I was very worried 19 because it was clear that if Slovenia could reject the 20 competence of the federation then other republics could as well, 21 Slovenia's rejection of the only political mechanism left, the 22 only political mechanism for resolving disputes between 23 republics, left nothing other than the unilateral actions of the 24 republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: There were two questions I would like to ask you, 26 Professor. The first one is we have heard a great deal from 27 individual witnesses about contentedly living together of 28 1 different ethnic groups, to the extent to which “my best friend 2 is a Serb” or “I am godfather to a Croat”. Contrasted with that is 3 the fact that we find that in villages in the opstina Prijedor 4 they seem to be very clearly designated and understood by 5 everyone as being Muslim villages or Serbian villages or Croat 6 villages. How do you, if you do, reconcile those two views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In two ways. The greatest interminglings of populations in the 8 former Yugoslavia were in cities and in the province of 9 Vojvodina in Serbia, and in parts of Croatia that actually 10 boarded Bosnia and Herzegovina areas called Banija and 11 Slavonia. I suppose I could point to them on a map if you 12 wished. In rural Bosnia and in some other rural parts of the 13 country the traditional pattern had been that you would have 14 Serb villages, Muslim villages, Croats villages, whatever, and 15 there was much less intermingling and yet as the 1980s 16 progressed, I mean as Yugoslavia became more prosperous, you 17 know, people had cars, people would go from villages, they would 18 go to Prijedor, they would go to Banja Luka, they would go to 19 Sarajevo, went to university. They did mingle and this form of 20 identity was not a primary form of identity to most people in 21 the 1980s. I can also tell you that the nationalist movements did 23 not arise in the regions, the republics or the regions within 24 republics that were most mixed. They arose in the regions that 25 were most homogenous. Slovenia, for example, or in Croatia the 26 heartland of the HDZ was not in the mixed regions of Banija and 27 Slavonia, but was in the regions that were almost purely Croat. 28 1 Similarly, the Serbian Party in Croatia, the SDS, was based in 2 the part of Croatia, in Knin, that was and had been for 3 centuries virtually entirely Serb. Nationalists in those homogenous areas more or less 5 drove the politics, and to the detriment of the people living 6 together, living intermingled, who in one sense could not 7 believe that these things could happen but on the other sense 8 could believe that these things could happen. If I may give an 9 example, in the Croatian elections in 1990 the people in the 10 mixed regions were Serbs and Croats were living together and 11 intermarrying did not vote overwhelmingly for the nationalist 12 parties. But, 28 what drove the discussion was the politics of, on the one hand, Croatian historians saying that, you know, this had all been overblown and, on the other hand, Serbs saying it had all been underplayed, and serious scholarly work tended to get lost in the cross-fire. 6 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Did you say that, I do not know how to pronounce it ---- 8 A. Jasenovac. 9 Q. J-A-N-E-S-O-V-A-C? 10 A. Close. J-A-S-E-N-O-V-A-C. 11 Q. That was located in the Prijedor region, was it not? 12 A. Well, it was actually located across the river in Croatia, Sana River. 14 Q. But north west, I guess? 15 A. Yes, I would have to look at the map to know exactly where it is, but, yes, it is close by. 17 Q. Not too far? 18 A. Yes, it is reasonably close by. 19 Q. You said that camp was run by Jews? 20 A. I did not say that, no. I say that President Tudjman suggests that in a portion of the 1990 edition of his book which, I understand, has since been removed. 23 Q. Was that the thesis he wrote at the university or what was it? 24 A. No, it was a book that he wrote, that Dr. Tudjman is now in his 70s, this is a book that he wrote in the late 1980s. It is a very interesting read, I can assure you. 27 MR. NIEMANN: But, in any event, the wildly inflated figures given of 28 the number of dead primarily suited the Serbian interests who may have wanted to stir up nationalistic feelings among the population; is that not right? 4 A. Sure, just as the raising the number of -- in the first place bringing in the category of Croats killed by the partisans and then raising that as high as possible serves an interest of Croatian leaders at the time. Yes, I wrote a quite substantial article about all of this called "Recounting the Dead", which I do not know if you have, but I will send you one. 10 Q. Thank you. The type of constitutional nationalism that you spoke of in the 1990s, was it a similar type of Constitutional nationalism that operated in Serbia? 13 A. I am sorry? 14 Q. Was it a similar type of constitutional nationalism that operated in Serbia as opposed to when compared to the other republics of Croatia and Slovenia? 17 A. Constitutionally, it is harder to find in Serbia, although one certainly does find it in the preamble to the Serbian Constitution, which I cite in what we exhibited, the article that is supposedly on the streets now, and I believe I cited in the articles that you are looking at. Certainly, one found it most openly expressed in the Croatian Constitution. Serbia, however, Serbian politics seemed less tightly bound to constitutional norms than, perhaps, in other places. 25 Q. Why is that? 26 A. The Serbian political structure in many ways did not change overly from the socialist period. It is many of the same 28 people. 2 Q. Moving on to Bosnia and Herzegovina itself, you say in an article that is entitled "Nationalism in former Yugoslavia"? 4 A. It is entitled? 5 Q. I apologise, "Constitutional Nationalism" ---- 6 A. Right. 7 Q. --- "in the former Yugoslav Republics". You say: "Until late 1992 Constitutions in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not reflect constitutional nationalism", what do you mean by that? 10 A. Well, my formulation of constitutional nationalism, which I have forgotten exactly the page number in there, but I do define it, it is a constitutional and legal structure that privileges one narod, nation, ethnically defined over others in the state. I say that you do not find this in Bosnia and Herzegovina because you do not have a single majority narod who can be in that privileged position. Instead, you have got the three narodi and then the nationalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that it was not possible to devise a constitutional structure that would do that. 20 Q. But why did you say until late 1992? 21 A. I am not sure. When did I actually publish that article? The date of is 1992. Did I stop then or did something happen that I am trying to remember five, four years later? 24 Q. It appears to be published in the winter of 1992. 25 A. Right. Well, there is a little -- I am sure it came out in 1993 with a cover date of 1992. If that is what you are referring to, I would, presumably, have stopped there because that, you 28 know, is when I had to get it back to the publisher. 2 Q. I see. So you are not suggesting that there was some sort of change in late 1992? 4 A. I do not remember -- certainly not for the Bosnian Constitution in 1992. I am not suggesting that. I think I am just stopping. 6 Q. In the same article, you go on to say: "While the leaders of the group agreed to share power at the level of the opstina, the victorious party of the majority ethnic group took absolute control over local government purging all not of their nation", this is referring specifically to Bosnia-Herzegovina? 11 A. Right. 12 Q. Are you saying this is a general thing or are you saying there are exceptions to it? 14 A. I imagine there probably are exceptions to it, but I was writing on the basis of the information available to me at the time. However, I might add that I believe it is the 1994 Country Reports of the US State Department on Bosnia-Herzegovina said that in the areas controlled by the SDA it is absolutely one Party rule, and in the areas controlled by the HDZ it is absolutely one Party rule, and thus monoethnic rule. The State Department thinks highly of those folks. I mean, those are friends. So I think it is a pattern that by the reports apparent to me in 1992, from sources that seemed credible to me, seemed true, and it certainly rings true with what has happened since then. 26 Q. But you would not be surprised to hear that there was, at least that we know of, one exception to that? 28 1 A. No, I would not be surprised at an exception, no. 2 Q. In the same article you speak of democracy being still birth especially and you say specifically in Serbia as a consequence of this nationalism. Do you agree with that? 5 A. The project I am working on now, as I said at the start of my testimony, is actually called "Potemkin Democracies, Serbia and Croatia since 1990", so yes. 8 Q. I raised with you earlier the question of propaganda and particularly propaganda in Serbia. It is true, is it not, that Milosevic in Serbia took a particular type control over media? 11 A. Milosevic in Serbia was the first to take particularly tight control over the media in a Yugoslav Republic, and it was a recipe that was followed by the HDZ government as soon as it took power. So, he was one of, yes, and certainly freedom of the media is not a characteristic that we associate with the region where people speak Serbo-Croatian. 17 Q. You also spoke in your evidence of moves being taken by Slovenia in relation to, if I can express it this way, upsetting the constitutional arrangement by making amendments and so forth. Did Slovenia do that on its own, I think as you suggested first, or was it provoked into this by other events that happened in Serbia? 23 A. Well, as I said yesterday, what you have with the demise of state socialism in the former Yugoslavia, because I think this is one where I started yesterday, you have the question arising of what will replace state socialism, and you have the rise of nationalist movements as well as people attempting to promote a 28 1 type of liberal democracy that we would recognise in western 2 Europe. So that these efforts are going on. I am afraid I have 3 lost my train of thought. I am sorry. What was your question 4 again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you whether the events in Slovenia ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, right. I am sorry. The Slovenes are, indeed, part of 7 this. So the reason I was introducing the comments of the 8 Slovenian intellectuals yesterday and recounting my own 9 experiences in Slovenia in the late 1980s was that nationalism 10 was certainly rising in Slovenia, and nationalism rising in 11 Slovenia was rising at the same time as some people were 12 speaking of it in Serbia, and this is before the arrival of 13 Slobodan Milosevic; the discussions in the Exhibit, the pages 14 from Dnevni Telegraf, the discussions that took place before 15 Milosevic arrived on the scene. Milosevic certainly was the first to take power with a 17 nationalist tinge to it, but followed by Slovenes. When we are 18 talking about the constitutional processes, constitutionally it 19 was clear to me in the summer of 1989 when I obtained the draft 20 of the Slovenian Amendments that if these Amendments were valid, 21 then Yugoslavia was invalid. This seemed to me to be extremely 22 dangerous, because if the Yugoslav federation, the federal 23 organs, were to cease to exist, there are no mechanisms then for 24 resolving conflicts between republics and that is, indeed, what 25 happened. I actually published (along with a colleague from the 27 Belgrade Law School) an article setting out this scenario. It 28 was first thing I ever published in a Yugoslav newspaper. It was a short article in Borba in September of 89. 3 Q. Would you agree with me, with the proposition, that there was growing hostility between Serbia and Slovenia in 1989? 5 A. Yes, certainly. 6 Q. This arose, among other things, out of what was happening in Kosovo? 8 A. Yes, certainly there was increasing hostility between Serbia -- I am sorry Serbia and Slovenia throughout 1989, yes. 10 Q. Would you agree with me that this hostility between Serbia and Slovenia was instrumental in the passing of the Amendments to the Slovenian Constitution? 13 A. I am sure it had a lot to do with it. It was part of the political climate at the time, yes, absolutely. 15 Q. Would you agree with the word "instrumental"? 16 A. Yes, I am sure because it was a very important part of the political climate of Slovenia at the time. 18 Q. Had Slobodan Milosevic captured the Serbian media by 1987? 19 A. By the end of '87, yes -- most of the Serbian media, the most important media, the most important daily papers and the television station, yes. It is curious that Serbia has until this day maintained a couple of independent media, but they are of limited circulation but superb quality. 24 Q. Speaking of the elections in Serbia in 1990, were they seen as fair and free elections in the same way as they were seen as elections in the other parts of what was the former Yugoslavia? 27 A. I believe the phrase used by international observers was "free 28 but not fair" because of the control over the media. 2 Q. Indeed, opposition rallies were not covered by the media and there are misquotes and things of that nature? 4 A. Yes. 5 Q. As a result of that election, Slobodan Milosevic captured 194 of the 250 votes? 7 A. Yes, his Party did, yes, the Socialist Party of Serbia, yes. 8 Q. The implementation of the process of ethnic cleansing that occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina, would you agree with me that that impacted most severely and extensively upon the non-combatant civilian community? 12 A. The non-combatant civilian community has certainly suffered the most in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have not concentrated on the processes of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina. 15 Q. Would you agree with me that what occurred there was aided by paramilitary groups, including those controlled by Seselj? 17 A. I am now -- you are now asking questions that I am less confident on, but I believe those were the reports at the time. 19 Q. Do you see a parallel between what occurred in Nazi Germany in the period of 1930 up to 1940 and this process of what was occurring with nationalism, with the emergence of dominant ethnic groups in Yugoslavia in the 1990s? 23 A. I am not sure what you mean by a "parallel" here. I find that nationalism of this type, associating nation, narod, ethnic group in American terms, with state, which is a territory and a government, to be a very central European formula. I do not read German. My colleagues who do tell me that this Germany 28 constitutional thought goes this way. Of course, you see this in the citizenship laws of Germany. What I have been looking at in my work, citizenship laws are part of it and discriminatory citizenship laws and certainly denaturalising, if you will, people who had been citizens of a state, as has happened to Jews in Germany in 1934, as happened to people in the post Yugoslav republics, and this is certainly part of it. It is all part of the image of who actually belongs in the state, whose state it is. I am not sure if that is what you are referring to? 11 Q. Yes. Do you say that that has its foundations in these Constitutions? 13 A. I say that these Constitutions put forth a vision of the state that is congruent with that image. It depends on how far it is then taken. Conceptually, those who are not of the majority nation do not really belong in the state. It is not theirs. I mean, that is why they are not part of the sovereign group. 18 Q. Is that part of the constitutional framework or is it more correct to say that it was part of the political philosophy of the nationalist parties at the time? 21 A. I actually view it as a cultural logic. 22 Q. You may do, but is it reflected through the political process, is the point that I am raising, such as, for example the HDZ, the SDS or the SDA in Bosnia-Herzegovina? 25 A. It is certainly reflected in who wants to join these parties. It may also be reflected in what happens after the election. I have viewed some of the processes that have taken place after 28 these elections as being an inversion of what Americans call affirmative action, negative action, if you will. The point of the state is certainly not to ensure equality of an equal body of citizens. It is to ensure the superior status of the majority nation. This is where in very many ways that frequently people would lose rights, would lose employment, would lose ultimately the right to citizenship on an ethno-national basis. This is very logical if you come into this framework of thought. It is not a logic that I like, but it is a logic that I try to identify. 11 Q. But would you agree with me if I put to you that particularly, say, in Bosnia-Herzegovina this was directed more as a political philosophy, for example, of the SDS, rather than there being any specific constitutional measures in operation? 15 A. Well, I see the SDS and the HDZ, particularly, as being very similar in these structures. 17 Q. For the sake of balance, I am happy to include the HDZ, but I am saying would you agree with me that this is a political ---- 19 A. It is a political logic, yes. 20 Q. --- logic, yes? 21 A. Yes, it is political logic, yes. It is a very strong political logic. 23 Q. It certainly was not derived, was it, from the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina? 25 A. From a constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina? 26 Q. Yes. 27 A. No, no, no, not from the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina 28 which was written and amended under state socialism, and no new Constitution was ever written for Bosnia and Herzegovina, unless we now count the Dayton Constitution, but that was not written by people from Bosnia and Herzegovina. 5 Q. It would not be under the Constitution of Serbia either? 6 A. No, you can see the logic reflected in whose state it is in the preamble. The Serbian Constitution defines Serbia as a state of equal citizens in probably Article 1. 9 Q. Nor would it be Croatia in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina? 10 A. I am sorry, I did not understand the question. 11 Q. What I am saying is that the political structure which would see the bringing about of the domination and exclusion of the other non-ethnic group is not reflected in the Croatian Constitution in terms of what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina? 15 A. I am not sure of the connection with Bosnia and Herzegovina. I interpret the Constitutions in part in the context of what the politicians are saying. It may not be expressed in the Croatian Constitution, but it is clearly expressed whose state it is. Mr. Tudjman has been very clear about whose state it is. 20 Q. Yes, but not in relation specifically when dealing with the constitutional provisions of Croatia could that apply to the political activities of the Parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina is my point. 24 A. Well, in so far as the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina is controlled by the HDZ of Croatia, and it is, are we in a constitutional framework here? 27 Q. Are you saying that we are? 28 1 A. Well, I do not know. I mean, supposedly we are not, and yet it was the HDZ in Zagreb that was able to change the leader of the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina in early -- in late April/early May of 1992, replacing Mr. Kljuic with Mr. Boban, and the comment was that Mr. Kljuic had proved to be too much Bosnian and not enough Croatian. Is that within the constitutional structures? I would doubt it very much. Is that the political reality? Yes, it is. 9 Q. That is, essentially, what I am suggesting to you ---- 10 A. OK. 11 Q. --- that it is political rather than constitutional. With the position in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think you described it as being stillborn, is that correct? 14 A. I said ---- 15 Q. You described it as ----- 16 A. --- the still birth of democracy is a term that I have used a number of times. I have used it in regard to the former Yugoslavia. I may have used in regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina. I see various similar processes happening in Yugoslavia and then in Bosnia. 21 Q. What do you mean by that? What do you mean by the term "stillborn" in relation to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina? 23 A. I believe you saw, you heard this morning that if I applied Mr. Badinter's criteria to Bosnia and Herzegovina, by the time it was recognised it was non-empirically a state. It was a state in the process of dissolution, to use Mr. Badinter's wonderful phrase. Unfortunately, it got there as a result of 28 elections that were free and fair. It has been one of the tragedies of those of us who have dealt with Yugoslavia for a long time that the country that we saw becoming increasingly open, increasingly democratic, in the 1980s, so much of it after -- which leading to the first free elections has become so much less so as the time has gone past -- this is through the looking glass feeling that one gets if one has been there, that it goes more and more like the -- the various parts of it grow more and more like the Eastern Europe that it had not been since 1965. I think in that sense we could say that most of the elections in Yugoslavia in 1990 were "free and fair", and then we can pronounce them democratic. But, as somebody has said, it does not take one election to have a democracy, it takes at least two, and free and fair -- two free and fair elections in the territories of the former Yugoslavia are hard to find and certainly not to be found in Serbia, Croatia or Bosnia. 18 Q. But, even accepting that there is no democracy, if one accepts that, in any of those places, that does not mean to say the state does not exist, does it? 21 A. I applied Mr. Badinter's criteria to the existence of the state. 22 Q. His definition? 23 A. Well, his definition provided criteria. 24 Q. I think you told us this morning or it was read to you this morning what that definition was. Perhaps you might tell us the definition that you apply? 27 A. Well, as I recalled, Mr. Badinter in the first opinion described 28 a state as a community in a territory subject to organised political authority, and suggested that one needed to look to the Constitutional order to determine the sway of control over the population in the territory. 5 Q. Do you regard that as being sufficient? 6 A. I regard it as a quite useful definition. I would be perfectly happy to entertain further definitions. 8 Q. I mean, that seemingly could apply to a city council, could it not? 10 A. Again, if may quote Mr. Badinter, which is all I can do here, he regarded the existence of the state as an empirical question on which recognition was not a deciding factor. I mean, if one looks ---- 14 Q. Of course, at the time he was dealing with the whole issue of recognition? 16 A. I recognise this, yes. I recognise the recognition. Well, political theorists have written volumes over the definition of the state. I am not a political theorist. 19 Q. But you are the one that posited or said you accept this definition, and that is what I am exploring, but you would agree with me, would you not, the fact that you may not exercise control over the whole part of the state or, indeed, that a part of the population of the state is not necessarily represented in the legislative process, is not of itself a factor which would bring about the non-existence or death of a state? 26 A. Not of itself necessarily, no. 27 Q. There are numerous examples of this. 28 1 A. I am sorry? 2 Q. There are numerous examples of this. I mean, you have Sri Lanka and the Tamils? 4 A. Yes, you have Sri Lanka and the Tamils. 5 Q. Cyprus and the Turks? 6 A. You have Cyprus and the Turks. 7 Q. Israel and the occupied territories? 8 A. Yes, there are many, many examples, certainly. 9 Q. But nobody suggests for one minute that they are not states, do they? 11 A. Well, I think there is a difference. Certainly Cyprus existed as a single independent state for a period before the government lost control of part of the territory, as did Sri Lanka, of course. So what you have then is an established government that loses control over a portion of the territory -- an established government of a state that can be recognised as an independent state for a while. Bosnia and Herzegovina, as an independent state, however, never had control. In fact, the recognised government of Bosnia and Herzegovina does not have control over either western Herzegovina or the Republika Srspka and it has not, so that this was recognition of a state as a state of a territory, large portions of the population of which rejected inclusion in that state which strikes me -- that is why I have said that recognition of the state had to mean war, because if it is to be realised in the territory that it is recognised, it has to be imposed on the parties that reject it or, having made clear that 28 they reject it, they would also fight to avoid being included within it which is where I believe I ended this morning. 3 Q. You are not suggesting, are you, that the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have control over the whole of the peoples and the whole of the territories of that state for some considerable period? 7 A. Not as an independent state, certainly. 8 Q. No, but I am asking you the question, they did exercise control over the peoples and territory of that state, did they not, the Republic? 11 A. As a Republic within Yugoslavia, yes, a control that began to break down, as Yugoslavia was breaking down, but only as a Republic within the control of, within the framework, rather, of Yugoslavia, yes. 15 Q. That framework, of course, had broken down, the framework of SFRY, a considerable period earlier. I think we posited the date 15th May 1991, but you suggested it was even earlier than that? 19 A. It was breaking down, yes, and it was breaking for -- its breakdown was repeated, essentially, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We remember that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was also a state recognised by the United Nations. In fact, it was a founding member of the United Nations and a founding Member of the League of Nations before it, but that did not make it empirically a state to Mr. Badinter in December 1991, and if apply his criteria to Bosnia it was not either on the day it was recognised. 28 1 Q. But the international community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they not? 3 A. Yes. 4 Q. It declared its independence on 6th March 1992? 5 A. Well, but here you have the problem with "it proclaimed its independence" but its, "its", existence for one and the competence of those who claim to speak for all of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina were both being challenged by the leadership, the elected leadership, of at least one of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, this represented, as I tried to go through today at some considerable pains, a breakdown of the constitutional structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself as the constitutional structure of Yugoslavia had broken down. 15 Q. But these factors all go to the determination of whether a place is a state or not, a territory is a state or not, you agree with me? 18 A. It is a shame Mr. Badinter said that this was an empirical question. I was treating it as an empirical question. 20 Q. It is also recognised by Croatia, is it not? 21 A. It is officially recognised by Croatia, yes. 22 Q. And by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? 23 A. Well, I believe that was one of the clauses in the Dayton Agreement that there is actually a mutual recognition clause, so if that is in the Dayton Agreement (as I believe it is), it would have been effective in December of '95. 27 Q. Since 1992 until the present, Bosnia and Herzegovina 28 participates in the international community as a state? 2 A. Yes. 3 Q. It is accepted by the international community as a state? 4 A. Yes. 5 Q. It has embassies that operate around the world? 6 A. Certainly. 7 Q. It continues to function with government, with President and all the apparatus of a state? 9 A. Yes, this is true. 10 Q. So, having regard to all of that, are you suggesting that it is no longer a state? 12 A. Empirically, the recognised government of Bosnia-Herzegovina has control of approximately 30 per cent of the territory of the state and has never had control over much more than that, and never had control over much more than that when it was recognised as a state. I mean, you know, we can discuss this for a long time. The problem here has been that so many of the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not themselves recognise it as a state. Whether we choose to do so or not, they did not and they were acting in the context of the breakdown of the constitutional organs, the constitutional system, that had existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina up to that time. I mean, I do not know if we could turn it around and propose that the international community could suddenly recognise something as a state and it would thereby be a state. That is actually the logic of your position. I am sure that 28 1 there is something in the middle, but by Mr. Badinter's 2 criteria, those that were used to say that the Socialist Federal 3 Republic of Yugoslavia was in a state of dissolution, so was 4 Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The international community went this way, did it not, because 6 the borders of the state were the borders of the original 7 Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The border is on map. There is a very curious situation if one 9 had been in the former Yugoslavia before all of this. The 10 borders were not usually marked. You did not necessarily know 11 when you crossed from one Republican to another unless you 12 happen to know the place names or there is a change in script. 13 It is not like the United States. If one crosses from New 14 Jersey into Pennsylvania, there is a large sign that says 15 "Welcome to Pennsylvania" and gives you the name of the 16 governor. But there was not anything like that in Bosnia and 17 Herzegovina. So that actually the position that existing borders 19 were being recognised was actually a demand that de facto new 20 borders should be created, because the border was, essentially, 21 meaningless on the ground. It, obviously, has administrative 22 importance, you know, where you pay your taxes and where you 23 vote. But, for other purposes, it was not particularly 24 important. Suddenly the transformation of these administrative 25 borders into, in an attempt to translate, into international 26 borders was, in effect, creating new borders. If these were 27 rejected by the people on the ground, as they were by the Croats 28 of Herzegovina and the Serbs of Bosnia, then what do we do? 2 Q. But the opstinas of Bosnia-Herzegovina were clearly defined, were they not? People knew where their opstina was. 4 A. Sure. 5 Q. Which opstina they lived in? 6 A. Of course. 7 Q. They knew that those opstinas were in a particular Republic? 8 A. That is right. I mean, clearly the borders were there as defined as certainly administrative borders. Absolutely. There is no question about it. But did you not have to stop and show your passport which would make it a physical barrier, and that is what would have to be created. 13 Q. You do not have stop and show your passport coming into Holland from Germany anymore either, but that does not mean to say the Netherlands is not a state, does it? 16 A. Right, but this is a very curious dynamic because at the same time that the European Community is saying it is perfectly all right to create new physical borders in the Balkans, we are removing borders. That was very odd. I mean, the whole treatment of this by the European Community was very odd. 21 Q. But it was not only the European Community, was it? 22 A. I am sorry? 23 Q. It was not only the European Community? 24 A. No, no, the United States of America was certainly involved in all of this, yes. 26 Q. So it was just not limited to that. Would you agree with me that the recognition of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 28 United States and by the European Community turned the conflict in that country into an international armed conflict? 3 A. An interesting question, Mr. Niemann. Well, it is an interesting question. Let me give you a counter. In early 1991, the Foreign Minister of Italy, Mr. Dimichaelos(?), told the Slovenes and the Croats that, "If you folks secede, you are going to cause a war and we are going to put a wall around Yugoslavia, and when you have stopped killing each other we will deal with you". Now, had that been the stance of the international community, certainly no one would have said that this was an international conflict. If you are saying that the pronunciation by however we define the international community turns a civil war into an international conflict, I suppose that one could well argue that. I suspect it is not going to have much effect on what is motivating the people in a civil war. 17 Q. Maybe not, but you certainly accept it as so, do you not? 18 A. I am sorry? 19 Q. You certainly accept it as so that the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina turned the conflict, transformed it, into an international conflict? 22 A. I am not sure that I do actually. 23 Q. If I can just ---- 24 A. I think I know you may be referring to my response to a critic, a letter in the Slavic Review that was written in probably early 1993. 27 Q. I am referring to two articles which you wrote. One, The 28 Yugoslav Collapse, National Suicide and Foreign Assistance? 2 A. Yes, which I wrote as it was taking place ---- 3 Q. You say ---- 4 A. --- with less time for reflection than one might ---- 5 Q. If I might just quote what you said? 6 A. By all means. 7 Q. "With the recognition of the independence of Slovenia and Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and their acceptance of the United Nations, the European Community and the United States legally transformed the civil war into international conflict". 11 A. I think I wrote that in approximately May of 1992 and I believe I rethought my composition. 13 Q. So you have changed your mind on that matter? 14 A. Well, I have done a bit more research. 15 Q. What about an article you wrote called The Bosnian Debacle? Are you aware of that? 17 A. Yes, of course. 18 Q. That is a much more resent article, is it not? 19 A. Yes. 20 Q. How recent is that? 21 A. Sorry? 22 Q. How recent is that article? 23 A. 19 -- early '95, early '94. 24 Q. Only you say on page 14 of that article: "The legal effect of the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to transform a civil war into an international conflict"? 27 A. Well, as part of a rhetorical structure, I had not actually done 28 much research on that aspect of it. It certainly was not key to the thrust of either the 1992 article or the 1994 article. One does sometimes put in material that might be viewed as dicta rather than holding in an academic article as well. 5 Q. So are you telling us now that this is no longer your view, you do not hold this view any more? 7 A. No, I do not think I do hold that view any more. 8 Q. Are there any other views you have had told us about in the course of your evidence that you do not hold to be true any more? 11 A. I do not believe so. I will stick to the evidence as I presented it. I might remind you that Lord Caines was once asked if he had changed his mind, and he said: "When I obtain new information I change my mind. What do you, sir?" 15 Q. I see. So it is on the basis of further information, is it, that you change your mind? 17 A. Further information and thought. I have been working on this for quite a while, as you, apparently, have had the dubious pleasure of seeing. 20 Q. Perhaps you might tell us what matters or factors you have taken into account which influence you to change your mind? 22 A. On this particular point? 23 Q. Yes. 24 A.
